title: The product rule as a growing rectangle
examples: Why does the product rule work?
What is the product rule in calculus?
Is the derivative of a product the product of the derivatives?

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

explain.say: Imagine a vegetable garden in Kenya, 10 metres long and 6 metres wide. Its area is 10 times 6, which is 60 square metres. Look at the biggest block: that is the old area. Now you make both sides a little longer. How much area do you gain?

draw.text: The product rule as a growing rectangle

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

explain.say: Stretch the length by half a metre. You gain a strip along the 6 metre side: 6 times 0.5, which is 3 square metres. See this small block? That strip is width times the change in length.

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

explain.say: Now stretch the width by half a metre too. That adds a strip along the 10 metre side: 10 times 0.5, which is 5 square metres. Can you see it is a bit bigger than the first strip? Why do you think it is?

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

explain.say: There is one more piece, a tiny corner: 0.5 times 0.5, just 0.25. Look how small it is! When the changes shrink towards zero, the corner vanishes much faster than the strips. So only the two strips count.

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

explain.say: So the change in area is u times change in v plus v times change in u. That is the product rule! Well done. Check: 10.5 times 6.5 is 68.25, which is exactly 60 plus 3 plus 5 plus 0.25.

items.label: Corner 0.5×0.5
items.ask: Why is the corner piece ignored?

faq.a: To differentiate u times v, you do u times the derivative of v, plus v times the derivative of u. In short: d of uv equals u dv plus v du.
asks: What is the formula for the product rule?

faq.a: When a rectangle with sides u and v grows a little, it gains a strip u times the change in v and a strip v times the change in u. These are the two terms of the product rule.
asks: Where do the two terms come from?

faq.q: Why is the corner piece ignored?
faq.a: The corner is the change in u times the change in v, two tiny numbers multiplied. As the changes shrink to zero it gets small much faster than the strips, so it disappears from the derivative.
asks: Why does the small corner not count?

faq.q: Is the derivative of a product the product of the derivatives?
faq.a: No. For x times x, the derivative is 2x, but the product of the derivatives is 1 times 1, which is 1. You need the product rule.
asks: Can I just multiply the derivatives?

faq.q: How do you use the product rule on x squared times sin x?
faq.a: Let u be x squared and v be sin x. Then the derivative is x squared times cos x plus sin x times 2x.
asks: What is the derivative of x^2 sin x?

facts: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx.
A 10.5 m by 6.5 m rectangle has area 68.25 m², which is 60 + 3 + 5 + 0.25.

quiz.say: A rectangle has sides 8 and 5. Both grow by 0.1. Which strip adds more area?
quiz.show: A rectangle has sides 8 and 5. Both grow by 0.1. Which strip adds more area?
quiz.why: The strip along the 8 side is 8 × 0.1 = 0.8; the other is 5 × 0.1 = 0.5.

wrong.2: The longer side gives the bigger strip.

quiz.say: What is the derivative of x times x, using the product rule?
quiz.show: What is the derivative of x times x, using the product rule?
quiz.why: u dv + v du = x × 1 + x × 1 = 2x, the same as the derivative of x².

wrong.0: 1 is the product of the two derivatives, which is the mistake the rule fixes.
wrong.2: x counts only one of the two strips.
